clue.text: Anything tinned? Delicious starter: bird stuffed in bottom — way out!

parts.note: aught is an old word for anything, and putting it in a tin places it inside CAN

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so this takes the opening letter of the word Delicious
the bird is stuffed inside the word for bottom, as filling goes into a roast

parts.note: a bed is the bottom of a river or sea
an owl is a bird

explanation.surface: A diner rummages through tins, dreaming of a delicious stuffed bird, and gets told the idea is way out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out' is a cricket dismissal, not an exclamation of disbelief, where the bowler also takes the catch. 'Bottom' is a riverbed.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a batter is out caught and bowled when the bowler catches the ball, one of the ways of dismissal.

clue.text: Nanny is unable to — but ___ for container

definitions.text: Nanny is unable to — but ___ for container

parts.words: Nanny is unable to — but ___ for container
parts.note: a nanny goat is female and cannot, but the male goat, the ...: the two words together name a camping pot

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank puzzle about what a nanny cannot do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nanny' is a female goat, not a childminder; the male goat fills the blank, followed by 'can'. A billycan is a tin pot used for cooking over a campfire.
explanation.definitionFit: A billycan is a metal cooking pot with a lid and handle, a container used by campers in Australia and Britain.

clue.text: Award unblemished?

definitions.meaning: the statuette given by the film academy each year
split as ..., that is zero scars, which describes skin with no blemish

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a pun: O for nought plus SCAR gives 'no scar', so unblemished.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette is universally called by this nickname, so the award is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Doubly fine grass pulled up round back of hedge, twice

indicators.note: twice says the whole piece built so far is written two times in a row
round says the reversed grass goes around the hedge's last letter
in a down clue, pulled up means the word for grass is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: hay is dried grass

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, here the end of hedge

explanation.surface: Grass is pulled up around the back of a hedge twice, all very fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulled up' turns HAY into YAH, and 'round' wraps it around E, the 'back of' hedge, giving YEAH; 'twice' doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'yes, yes' twice over is a casual way of agreeing that something is fine or acceptable, so it is a doubled fine.

clue.text: See 11
Publication no longer appearing contemporary with easily manipulated hack — shabby about right?

parts.note: contemporary means new or modern
soft means pliable, easily manipulated
to hew is to hack or chop

indicators.note: about says the word for shabby goes round the letter for right

parts.note: old can mean worn and shabby

explanation.surface: A defunct paper is mocked as trendy, its pliant hack scruffy and right-wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is only a link. 'Hack' looks like a journalist, fitting the surface, but it is the verb meaning chop. 'about' puts R inside OLD for ORLD.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Sunday tabloid closed in 2011 after the phone-hacking scandal, so it is a newspaper no longer published.

clue.text: Poet in whom poetry?

definitions.meaning: the phrase 'poetry in ...' describes graceful movement, so this word is where the poetry is found

explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Motion was the UK's Poet Laureate from 1999 to 2009; the second half leans on the idiom 'poetry in motion'.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Motion is a British poet who served as Poet Laureate, so the surname names a poet.

clue.text: Susan, the agriculturist, makes you laugh out loud — it's the drugs!

indicators.note: out loud says the phrase about Susan is said aloud to give a word of the same sound

parts.words: Susan, the agriculturist, makes you laugh
parts.note: Susan is Sue, an agriculturist is a farmer, and making you laugh is tickling: Farmer Sue tickles

explanation.surface: A jolly farmer named Susan is so funny that someone suspects drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Said together, 'Farmer Sue tickles' runs into the word for medicinal drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pharmaceuticals are medicinal compounds, the products of the drug industry.

clue.text: Just too much pie, at best revolting

indicators.note: revolting suggests rising up and overturning, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A diner finds the pie, even at its best, revolting and a bit much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' rearranges PIE AT BEST, nine letters, into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something rather steep means it is excessive, especially a price or demand that goes a little too far.

clue.text: Remarkable time, hard to manage running backwards

indicators.note: running backwards says the pieces joined together are read from right to left

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
to cope is to manage

explanation.surface: A remarkable period proves hard to manage when run in reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running backwards' turns HCOPE, the whole run, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An epoch is a notable period marked by memorable events, a significant era.

clue.text: Big horrid giant's ideal pet, if hairy — is it?

definitions.text: Big horrid giant's ideal pet, if hairy — is it?

parts.words: Big horrid giant's ideal pet, if hairy — is it?
parts.note: the Biblical giant slain by David would suit a pet named after him: a huge hairy South American tarantula that preys on birds

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a horrid giant would choose a hairy pet.
explanation.walkthrough: The giant is the Philistine champion from the Bible; the creature named after him is the world's largest spider, a big hairy tarantula said to eat birds.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American tarantula is the largest spider by mass, enormous and hairy, a plausible pet for a horrid giant.

clue.text: Brief inspection initially poking bum

indicators.note: poking says the first letter pokes into the word for bum, sitting inside it

parts.note: a dosser is a tramp or bum, someone who sleeps rough

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the word inspection

explanation.surface: A short inspection begins with someone poking a backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' is a noun, a set of instructions or papers, not the adjective short; 'bum' is the vagrant, not the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A dossier is a file of papers on a case or person, which is what a lawyer's brief is.

clue.text: Food, one's gathered?

definitions.meaning: British school slang for snacks and sweets
a fold of cloth stitched to gather it in

explanation.walkthrough: TUCK is British schoolchildren's slang for food, especially sweets bought at a school tuck shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck means snacks in British slang, and in sewing a tuck is a gathered fold of fabric.

clue.text: Accord, perhaps binding last two characters from Stephen Fry novel for US actor

indicators.note: binding says the car maker wraps around the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: the Accord is a car model made by Honda

indicators.note: the final two letters of the word Stephen are taken
novel means new, so the letters of Fry are given a fresh order

explanation.surface: A deal binds Stephen Fry's novel for an American film star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accord' is a car model, not an agreement, and 'novel' is an anagram signal rather than a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fonda was an American film star of The Grapes of Wrath and Twelve Angry Men.

clue.text: Still silent about view? Not entirely

indicators.note: about says the word for silent goes round the shortened view

parts.note: quiet means silent

indicators.note: not entirely says the word for view loses its final letter

parts.note: a scene is a view

explanation.surface: A silent observer muses on a view, not wholly still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the adjective meaning motionless, not the adverb 'yet'; 'Not entirely' trims only the view.
explanation.definitionFit: Quiescent means inactive and at rest, the adjectival sense of still.

clue.text: Ultimate in rejection that hurts, partners claimed something unique

indicators.note: the ultimate in a word is its last letter, here from rejection
claimed says the cry of pain takes the partners inside it

parts.note: ouch is what you say when something hurts
N and S, north and south, are partners at bridge

explanation.surface: Rejection hurts in the end, and partners claimed it was unique.
explanation.walkthrough: North and South play as partners in the card game bridge, so NS stands for partners.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonsuch, an old word also spelt nonesuch, is a person or thing without equal.

clue.text: Very wriggly leech, one entering channel

indicators.note: entering says the letter for one goes into the jumbled leech
a wriggly leech twists about, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A very wriggly leech enters a channel of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' is the means by which something is expressed, not a waterway. 'wriggly' makes EHCLE from LEECH.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle in the figurative sense is a medium through which something is conveyed, as a channel is.

clue.text: Player, perhaps, underneath plant, sharp

indicators.note: underneath says, in a down clue, the golfer's name sits below the plant

parts.note: a vine is a climbing plant
Gary Player is a South African golfer, so Gary is an example of a Player

explanation.surface: Someone, perhaps a player, crouches beneath a sharp plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P is the giveaway: Player is Gary Player, the South African golf champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinegary means sour or acidic in taste, and figuratively sharp in manner.

clue.text: Quote something positive about it

indicators.note: about says the positive particle wraps around the word it

parts.note: a cation is a positively charged ion

explanation.surface: A quote says something positive about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something positive' is the chemists' cation, a positive ion, not praise; 'about' puts IT inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A citation is a quoted passage or reference, which is what a quote is as a noun.

clue.text: See 11
Top of chimney grabbed by roof worker slipping over, one's survived

indicators.note: grabbed by says the chimney's top letter is held inside the reversed worker
slipping over says the worker tumbles, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a tiler lays tiles on roofs

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, here from chimney

explanation.surface: A roofer slips over grabbing the top of a chimney, and survives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slipping over' turns TILER to RELIT, which grabs C from 'Top of' chimney.
explanation.definitionFit: A relict is a survivor, an organism or thing left from an earlier era, or archaically a widow.

clue.text: Artist seeing specialist, we hear, to avoid op?

indicators.note: to avoid says the letters op are left out of what is heard
we hear says the eye specialist's name is taken by its sound, with its middle consonant heard as a t

parts.note: an optician is an eye specialist
taken as written, short for operation

explanation.surface: Seeing a specialist in the hope of avoiding an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seeing' is a link. Said aloud, the eye specialist sounds like op-tishun; 'to avoid op' strips the first syllable, leaving the Venetian painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian was the great sixteenth-century Venetian painter.

clue.text: Most ethical part that shouldn't have been corrected

indicators.note: part says the answer is a portion of the words Most ethical

explanation.surface: The most ethical part ought to have been left uncorrected.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across 'Most ethical'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stet is the proofreader's mark meaning let it stand, telling a printer to undo a correction.

clue.text: See 6
Suggesting act unauthorised by the unions

parts.note: read as a clue, ... means the letters of cat run wild, and so suggests act

explanation.surface: Proposing some action that the unions have not approved.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'wild cat' would be wordplay for ACT, with 'wild' as an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A wildcat strike is one called without official union backing, so wildcat means unofficial.

clue.text: Knowing costing, devastated

indicators.note: devastated means wrecked, so the letters of costing are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shrewd is devastated at the cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devastated' rearranges COSTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnostic means relating to knowledge, especially secret spiritual knowledge.

clue.text: For whom time's passed, having discarded blue rosette?

parts.note: ex means former, something cast off
blue is the colour of the Conservatives, so a blue rosette marks a Con

explanation.surface: Someone has thrown away a blue prize rosette now the moment has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' is a prison sentence. In Britain the Conservative Party's colour is blue, and candidates wear rosettes in their party colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A former convict is someone who has served their prison time.

clue.text: Mug with which short contrary coquette fills a pond

indicators.note: fills says the reversed flirt goes inside the a-plus-pond piece

parts.note: a pool is a pond

indicators.note: contrary says the shortened word runs the opposite way
short says the word for coquette loses its last letter

parts.note: a coquette is a flirt

explanation.surface: A coquette fills a mug from the pond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with which' is a link. 'Mug' is a gullible person, not a cup; a coquette is a woman who flirts.
explanation.definitionFit: An April fool is someone tricked on April 1st, so a mug or dupe.
